newsitem.title: ANGOLA: U.N. concerned fighting could derail Angola peace.
newsitem.headline: U.N. concerned fighting could derail Angola peace.

text.p: The United Nations special envoy to Angola voiced concern about Angola's struggling peace process on Friday and said he had ordered a military investigation into fighting in the diamond-rich northeastern region.
A report on clashes between Angolan government and former rebel UNITA troops in Lunda Norte province would be released next week, Alioune Blondin Beye told Reuters.
A senior military source said on Thursday that both sides had thrown large numbers of troops into the battles, and the Angolan army was using tanks and artillery.
The fighting was described as the worst since a peace pact ended Angola's 20-year civil war in 1994.

U.N. force commander Phillip Sibanda, leading the mission, travelled to the mining town of Nzage on Friday where fighting has intensified. He has estimated that 14 government troops were killed and 90 wounded in clashes near there.
No figures were available on UNITA's casualties.

A mission including military attaches from the United States, Portugal and Russia -- the countries helping to oversee Angola's peace process -- travelled to other areas in the north to verify reports of UNITA troop movements.
Last year UNITA declared it had dismantled its guerrilla force and handed in all war materials, under U.N. supervision.
"I am waiting for our UNAVEM people, who are the only reliable people to me, to submit their reports and then we will take a position," Beye said.
Thousands of UNITA troops are reportedly returning to Angola from the former Zaire where they supported now deposed Mobutu Sese Seko, as close ally of UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi.
The Angolan government on the other hand backed the rebel forces of Laurent Kabila who ousted Mobutu and has declared himself president of the renamed Democratic Republic of Congo.
"The peace process is always a source of concern. When events started in Zaire eight months ago I followed situation because I knew the links between Zaire and Angola," Beye said in an interview.
"It is not by chance that I went eight times to Gbadolite (Mobutu's upc-country stronghold), so I was always aware that there were consequences," he added.

Beye, who has been leading the Angolan peace process since the signing of a 1994 peace treaty to end two decades of civil war, said he would discuss the outcome of the report with President Jose Eduardo dos Santos, who is currently in Italy, and UNITA's Savimbi.
"I am waiting for the results of the investigation. If investigators tell me there are soldiers from Zaire, then I will talk with the UNITA leadership," he said.

"We (U.N.) came here because the Angolans decided they wanted peace. If they decide to go back to war nobody can prevent them. We have only 6,000 blue helmets who cannot prevent 140,000 men from waging war," he said.
He said if the situation on the ground worsened, he would suggest to the Security Council the suspension of the peacekeepers' planned withdrawal from Angola which was due to be completed by August.

"We always said that our withdrawal plans depend on the situation on the ground. If the situation is good we can accelerate (the withdrawal). If it is very bad we can suggest that it stops...," he said.

He pointed out that in two years the Angolan peace process had made progress, with the formation of a government of unity, disarming of UNITA troops and the start of extension of state administration to the whole of the country.

Beye said the Angolan government had given the go-ahead for the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR to inspect thousands of refugees on Angola's northern border with Zaire, but permission was still needed from Kabila's government.
